questions.question: What are the essential Docker commands every developer should know?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can perform basic Docker operations independently without needing constant help from senior developers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Memorizing commands without understanding what they do — freshers often confuse images with containers or don't know when to use docker rm versus docker rmi
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention docker exec -it for debugging running containers — shows you've gone beyond just starting and stopping containers

questions.direct_answer: Essential commands: docker build creates images from Dockerfiles, docker run starts containers, docker ps lists running containers, docker stop/rm stops and removes containers, docker images lists local images, docker logs shows container output, and docker pull downloads images from registries.

rows: Build image from Dockerfile in current dir

answer_sections.content: The commands I use most day-to-day are: docker build -t myapp:1.0 . to build the image, docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp:1.0 to start it, docker ps to see what's running, and docker logs containerId to see what the app is printing. If I need to debug inside a container, docker exec -it containerId bash opens an interactive shell. docker stop and docker rm to clean up. The -d flag for detached mode runs the container in background — useful so the terminal isn't taken over by container logs. For working with compose, docker-compose up and docker-compose down replace most individual container management.

follow_up_questions: How do you view the last 50 lines of container logs?
What does docker exec -it container bash allow you to do?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app packaged as a Docker image
speakable_v2.hook: You don't need to memorize fifty Docker commands — knowing eight gets you through 95% of real development work.

items: docker build -t myapp:1.0 . — build an image from the Dockerfile in the current directory
docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp:1.0 — start a container and map the port
docker run -d myapp:1.0 — start in detached (background) mode so your terminal stays free
docker ps — see what containers are currently running
docker logs -f containerId — follow the app's log output in real time
docker exec -it containerId bash — open a shell inside the running container
docker stop / docker rm — stop and clean up a container
docker images — list all locally available images

beats.text: On a real team the most-used trio is docker run, docker ps, and docker logs. If the app isn't starting, docker logs shows the Spring Boot stack trace exactly as if you ran it locally.

speakable_v2.cap: candidates miss: forgetting -d means your terminal is locked to the container's log stream. Use -d for any container you plan to leave running and check separately with docker logs.

sections.title: Why Docker Commands Matter for Backend Developers
sections.content: Docker commands are your daily toolkit for packaging and running Java applications in isolated environments called **containers**. Think of Docker like a shipping container system: **images** are the blueprints (your packaged Spring Boot JAR plus its dependencies), and **containers** are the running instances created from those blueprints. Without Docker commands, you'd need senior devs to deploy every code change. Mastering these commands means you can build, test, and debug your microservices locally before pushing to staging. The core workflow: write code → build image → run container → check logs → iterate. Every backend team uses this flow dozens of times daily, so these commands become muscle memory quickly.

sections.title: Essential Docker Workflow for a Spring Boot Application
Key Points
content: **docker build**: Creates an image from a Dockerfile — the -t flag tags it with a name like order-service:v1.0 for easy reference
**docker run**: Starts a new container from an image — the -d flag runs it in background, -p maps ports, --name gives it a friendly identifier
**docker ps**: Lists running containers with their IDs, names, and ports — add -a to see stopped containers too
**docker logs**: Shows stdout/stderr from your application — use -f to follow in real time like tail, --tail 100 for last 100 lines
**docker exec -it**: Opens an interactive shell inside a running container — essential for checking files or running ad-hoc commands
**docker stop/rm**: Stops and removes containers — you must stop before removing, or use docker rm -f to force both
**docker images/rmi**: Lists and removes images — rmi needs all containers using that image to be removed first

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The essential Docker commands are build, run, ps, logs, stop, rm, images, and pull. I'll walk through the typical workflow. First, docker build creates an image from your Dockerfile — that's your packaged application. Then docker run starts a container from that image, and you'd use flags like -p to map ports so you can access it. Docker ps shows what's currently running, which is helpful when you have multiple containers. When something breaks, docker logs is your first debugging tool — it shows all the application output. If I need to dig deeper, docker exec -it lets me open a shell inside the running container to check files or run commands. Finally, docker stop gracefully shuts down a container, and docker rm deletes it. One thing that tripped me up early on: you can't remove an image with docker rmi if containers are still using it, even stopped ones. You need to docker rm the containers first. I also use docker pull to download images like Postgres or Redis from Docker Hub when I need them for local development. These commands cover probably ninety percent of daily work with Docker.

questions.question: What does docker run -p 8080:8080 mean?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that containers are isolated — without port mapping, you cannot access services running inside them from your host
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the container automatically exposes ports — freshers often forget -p and wonder why localhost:8080 doesn't work
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that you can map different ports like -p 9090:8080 to avoid conflicts if another service already uses 8080 on your host

questions.direct_answer: The -p flag maps ports from the host machine to the container. The format is -p host_port:container_port. So -p 8080:8080 means requests to localhost:8080 on your machine get forwarded to port 8080 inside the container where your Spring Boot app is listening.

answer_sections.content:
# host_port:container_port
docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp  # standard mapping
docker run -p 9090:8080 myapp  # host 9090 → container 8080
docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 8443:8443 myapp  # multiple ports

# Container runs on port 8080 internally (EXPOSE 8080)
# -p makes it accessible from outside the container

The -p flag maps a port on your host machine to a port inside the container. The format is host:container. So -p 8080:8080 means when you browse to localhost:8080, Docker forwards that request to port 8080 inside the container where Spring Boot is listening. The EXPOSE instruction in Dockerfile only documents which port the app uses — it doesn't actually publish it. The -p flag is what actually makes the port accessible from outside the container. If you run docker run without -p, the container runs but you can't access it from your browser.

follow_up_questions: What is the difference between EXPOSE in Dockerfile and -p in docker run?
How do you run a container and map port 80 on the host to port 8080 in the container?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app running in a container, accessed from the browser
speakable_v2.hook: Without the -p flag, your Spring Boot container runs perfectly — and you still can't reach it from your browser. Port mapping is the missing piece.

beats.text: The -p flag maps a port on your host machine to a port inside the container. Format is host_port:container_port. So -p 8080:8080 means requests to localhost:8080 on your machine are forwarded to port 8080 inside the container.
If you want Spring Boot running on container port 8080 but accessible on host port 9090, use -p 9090:8080. Your browser hits localhost:9090, Docker forwards it to container port 8080.

Containers are isolated by default. Their ports are not visible outside the container network. -p explicitly punches a hole from the host into the container. You can map multiple ports with multiple -p flags.

candidates miss: EXPOSE 8080 in the Dockerfile is just documentation — it does not publish the port. Only docker run -p actually makes the port reachable. This is one of the most common Docker gotchas for beginners.

speakable_v2.cap: Remember the format as 'outside:inside' — left side is what you type in your browser, right side is where the container is actually listening.

sections.title: Understanding Container Networking and Port Mapping
sections.content: Containers run in **isolated networks** by default — they can't be accessed from your host machine without explicit port mapping. The **-p flag** creates a bridge between a port on your host (your laptop) and a port inside the container. Think of it like forwarding calls: when someone dials your office number (host port), the receptionist forwards it to your desk extension (container port). Spring Boot apps typically listen on port 8080 inside the container. Without -p 8080:8080, that service is unreachable from your browser at localhost:8080 because the container's network is separate. The format is always host:container — the left side is where you connect from outside, the right side is where the app actually listens inside. You can map different ports to avoid conflicts: -p 9090:8080 means your app still listens on 8080 internally, but you access it at localhost:9090.

sections.title: Port Mapping Examples for Common Scenarios
Key Points
content: **-p flag syntax**: Always host_port:container_port — left side is your machine, right side is inside the container
**Container isolation**: Without -p, services inside containers are unreachable from your host — the container has its own network namespace
**Conflict resolution**: Use different host ports like -p 9090:8080 when multiple containers need to expose the same internal port
**Multiple mappings**: You can specify -p multiple times for apps with several ports — common for HTTP plus debugging or metrics endpoints
**localhost access**: After mapping, you access the service at localhost:host_port from your browser or other applications
**EXPOSE vs -p**: EXPOSE in Dockerfile is documentation only — it doesn't actually publish ports, you still need -p at runtime
**Binding to specific IPs**: Use -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 to restrict access to localhost only, preventing external network access

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Docker run -p 8080:8080 maps port 8080 on my host machine to port 8080 inside the container. The format is -p host_port:container_port. Containers are isolated by default, so without this mapping, I can't access the Spring Boot app running inside. The app listens on port 8080 internally, and the -p flag creates a bridge so requests to localhost:8080 on my machine get forwarded into the container. One thing that's really useful: I can map to different ports to avoid conflicts. If I already have something running on 8080, I can do -p 9090:8080 instead. That means the app still listens on 8080 inside the container, but I access it at localhost:9090 from my browser. I've used this when running multiple microservices locally — like an order service on 8080, a customer service on 8081, and a payment service on 8082. You can also map multiple ports at once, which is handy for debugging. For example, -p 8080:8080 -p 5005:5005 lets me attach a remote debugger to port 5005 while the HTTP API runs on 8080. A common mistake is forgetting the -p flag entirely and then wondering why localhost:8080 doesn't respond.

questions.question: How do you view logs from a running Docker container?

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can independently debug issues by reading application output — a core skill for containerized environments
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the -f flag for real-time logs — freshers often rerun docker logs repeatedly instead of following the stream
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention combining --since with --tail for targeted debugging like docker logs --since 5m --tail 50 to see recent errors without scrolling through gigabytes

questions.direct_answer: Use docker logs followed by the container ID or name. For example, docker logs order-api shows all output. Add -f to follow logs in real time like tail -f. Use --tail 100 to see only the last 100 lines, and --since 10m to see logs from the last 10 minutes.

answer_sections.content:
# See all logs
docker logs my-app-container

# Follow live (like tail -f)
docker logs -f my-app-container

# Last 100 lines
docker logs --tail 100 my-app-container

# Logs since 30 minutes ago
docker logs --since 30m my-app-container

# Get container ID first
docker ps  # shows container IDs

docker logs is essential for debugging. By default it shows all logs since the container started. I almost always use docker logs -f to follow the logs in real time — it stays open and shows new log lines as they appear, like tail -f on a log file. For a container that's producing a lot of logs, --tail 100 limits output to the last 100 lines so you don't get overwhelmed. If your Spring Boot app isn't starting correctly, docker logs will show the stack trace and tell you exactly what went wrong — same logs as if you ran it locally.

follow_up_questions: Where does Docker store logs on the host machine?
How do you configure Spring Boot to write structured JSON logs in Docker?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app failing to start inside a Docker container
speakable_v2.hook: When your containerized Spring Boot app silently fails, docker logs is the first place you look — and docker logs -f is the command you'll use every day.

beats.text: docker logs shows everything the application wrote to stdout and stderr since the container started. For a Spring Boot app, that's all the application log output — including stack traces, startup messages, and errors.

items: docker logs containerId — dump all logs since container started
docker logs -f containerId — follow live, like tail -f on a log file
docker logs --tail 100 containerId — only the last 100 lines
docker logs --since 30m containerId — logs from the last 30 minutes

beats.text: If a Spring Boot container crashes on startup, docker logs shows the full stack trace — same output as running the app locally. No guessing required.

speakable_v2.cap: non-obvious: if Spring Boot is writing logs to a file inside the container instead of stdout, docker logs will show nothing. Configure logging to stdout in container environments — that's where Docker expects to collect logs.

sections.title: Why Log Access Is Critical for Container Debugging
sections.content: **docker logs** is your primary debugging tool for containerized applications. Unlike traditional deployments where you might ssh into a server and read log files directly, containers treat **stdout and stderr as the logging interface**. When your Spring Boot app does System.out.println() or uses a logger like SLF4J, that output goes to the container's log stream, which Docker captures. Think of docker logs as a window into what's happening inside the sealed container. The basic command shows all accumulated logs, but real debugging power comes from flags like **-f** (follow in real time), **--tail** (show only recent lines), and **--since** (filter by time). When a production container crashes at 3 AM and restarts, being able to run docker logs --since 5m --tail 100 to see only the last five minutes before the crash is invaluable.

sections.title: Common Log Viewing Patterns for Troubleshooting
Key Points
content: **Basic usage**: docker logs container_name or container_id shows all output from stdout and stderr since the container started
**-f flag**: Follows logs in real time like tail -f — essential when watching for errors during testing or deployment
**--tail N**: Shows only the last N lines — use --tail 100 to avoid overwhelming output from long-running containers
**--since duration**: Filters logs by time — accepts values like 10m, 2h, or specific timestamps like 2024-01-15T14:30:00
**-t flag**: Adds timestamps to each log line — helps identify when errors occurred, especially for intermittent issues
**Combining filters**: Use --since with --tail for targeted debugging — docker logs --since 5m --tail 50 shows recent activity without gigabytes of old data
**Log retention**: Docker stores logs in JSON files on disk — containers with verbose logging can fill disk space over time

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To view logs from a running Docker container, I use docker logs followed by the container name or ID. For example, docker logs order-api shows all the output since that container started. If I want to watch logs in real time, I add the -f flag, which works just like tail -f. That's super helpful when I'm testing changes and want to see requests coming in immediately. For troubleshooting, I often combine flags. If a container has been running for days and has gigabytes of logs, I'll use --tail 100 to see just the last hundred lines. Or if I know an error happened recently, I'll do docker logs --since 10m to see only the last ten minutes. One pattern I use a lot is combining both: docker logs --since 5m --tail 50 gives me the last fifty lines from the past five minutes, which is perfect for diagnosing a recent crash. The -t flag adds timestamps to each line, which helps when I'm trying to correlate errors with specific requests. A mistake I made early on was rerunning docker logs over and over instead of using -f to follow the stream. Another tip: you can pipe to grep, like docker logs -f order-api | grep ERROR, to filter for specific patterns. That's really useful in production when there's tons of info-level logging.

questions.question: How do you clean up Docker resources (stopped containers, unused images)?

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness that Docker consumes significant disk space and needs regular maintenance — a practical operational skill often overlooked in tutorials
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing Docker caches layers aggressively — freshers are surprised when Docker uses 20GB after a few weeks of development
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention docker system df to check disk usage before cleanup — shows systematic approach to maintenance rather than blind pruning

questions.direct_answer: Use docker system prune to remove all stopped containers, unused images, and dangling build cache in one command. For targeted cleanup: docker container prune removes stopped containers, docker image prune removes unused images. To remove specific items: docker rm for containers, docker rmi for images.

answer_sections.content:
# Remove all stopped containers
docker container prune

# Remove unused images
docker image prune

# Remove EVERYTHING unused (nuclear option)
docker system prune
docker system prune -a  # also removes unused images

# Check disk usage
docker system df

Docker can eat up a lot of disk space if you don't clean up. Stopped containers, old images, and build cache accumulate. docker system prune removes stopped containers and dangling images in one shot. docker system prune -a is more aggressive and removes all images not currently used by a running container — useful on a laptop that's getting full. I run docker system df to see how much space Docker is using before deciding what to clean. On CI servers, cleanup scripts run automatically. On local machines, occasional docker system prune keeps things tidy.

follow_up_questions: What is a dangling image in Docker?
How do you automatically remove a container when it stops?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Developer laptop running low on disk space from accumulated Docker images
speakable_v2.hook: Docker is quietly accumulating stopped containers and old images on your machine — and you won't notice until your laptop's disk is full.

beats.text: Every docker build creates new image layers. Every docker run creates a stopped container when it finishes. Neither is cleaned up automatically. Over weeks of development, this adds up fast.

items: docker system df — check how much disk space Docker is using
docker container prune — remove all stopped containers
docker image prune — remove dangling images (untagged)
docker system prune — remove stopped containers, dangling images, and unused build cache
docker system prune -a — also removes images not used by any running container

beats.text: A dangling image is one that's been replaced by a newer build but still takes up space — its tag was reassigned to the new image and it now shows as none:none in docker images. docker image prune removes these.

production trap: docker system prune -a on a production machine removes all images not currently running — including images for services that are temporarily stopped. Use with care outside of local dev.

speakable_v2.cap: Run docker system prune periodically on your dev machine. On CI, cleanup jobs usually run automatically. Knowing the difference between prune and prune -a stops you from accidentally deleting needed images.

sections.title: Why Docker Resource Management Matters in Daily Development
sections.content: Docker aggressively **caches image layers** to speed up builds, but this consumes disk space rapidly. After a few weeks of development — building images, pulling base images like postgres:15, stopping containers without removing them — you can easily accumulate 20-40GB of Docker data. Think of Docker's storage like a workshop that never throws away scraps: every build leaves behind unused layers, every stopped container keeps its writable layer, and every pulled image version stays on disk. **docker system prune** is the master cleanup command that removes stopped containers, dangling images, and unused build cache in one shot. For targeted cleanup, **docker container prune** removes only stopped containers, while **docker image prune** removes unused images. Understanding when to prune aggressively versus preserving cache for build speed is a practical skill that separates developers who maintain healthy local environments from those who constantly run out of disk space.

sections.title: Comprehensive Docker Cleanup Workflow
Key Points
content: **docker system df**: Shows disk usage breakdown by images, containers, and build cache — run this first to see what's consuming space
**docker system prune**: Removes stopped containers, dangling images, and unused build cache — add -a to also remove unused tagged images
**docker container prune**: Removes only stopped containers — safer than system prune when you want to preserve images and cache
**docker image prune**: Removes unused images not referenced by any container — use -a to include tagged images that aren't currently in use
**docker rm vs docker rmi**: rm removes containers, rmi removes images — you must remove containers first before removing the images they use
**Build cache accumulation**: Docker caches every layer from every build — after weeks of development, this cache can grow to 10-15GB
**Pruning trade-off**: Aggressive pruning frees disk space but forces Docker to rebuild layers from scratch next time, slowing down builds

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: For Docker cleanup, I start by checking what's using space with docker system df. That shows me the breakdown of images, containers, and build cache. The nuclear option is docker system prune -a, which removes all stopped containers, unused images, and build cache in one shot. I use that when I'm really low on disk space. For more targeted cleanup, docker container prune removes just the stopped containers, which is useful after running lots of tests that create throwaway containers. Docker image prune removes unused images — those are images that no container is currently referencing. If I want to be more aggressive, docker image prune -a also removes tagged images that aren't in use. For specific items, docker rm removes a container by name or ID, and docker rmi removes an image. One thing to know: you can't remove an image if any containers are still using it, even stopped ones. You need to docker rm those containers first. A pattern I use is docker rm followed by the container name, then docker rmi for the image. Docker's caching is really aggressive, which is great for build speed but bad for disk space. After a few weeks of development, my Docker folder can hit twenty or thirty gigabytes. I run docker system prune maybe once a week to keep things under control. The trade-off is that pruning the build cache means my next build will be slower because Docker has to rebuild layers from scratch.

questions.question: How do you debug a running Docker container — what commands do you use?
questions.title: Debugging a Running Docker Container
questions.direct_answer: Use docker logs to see application output, docker exec -it to open a shell inside the container, and docker inspect to see container configuration and network details.

interviewer_intent.testing: Operational debugging ability — a developer who cannot diagnose a broken container is helpless on a real team
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing docker exec — many freshers only know how to start/stop containers
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention docker stats for real-time CPU/memory usage — shows awareness of performance debugging

sections.title: Essential Docker Debugging Techniques for Production Issues
sections.content: Debugging containerized apps requires a different mindset than traditional servers. You can't just ssh in and poke around — containers are **ephemeral and isolated**. The debugging workflow centers on three commands: **docker logs** for application output, **docker exec** for interactive access, and **docker inspect** for configuration details. Think of it like debugging a black box: logs tell you what the app is saying, exec lets you look inside, and inspect shows you how the box is configured. When a Spring Boot container won't start, you first check logs for stack traces. If the app starts but behaves weirdly, you exec into the container to check environment variables or file permissions. If network issues occur, inspect reveals IP addresses and port bindings. Advanced debugging includes **docker stats** for real-time resource usage and **docker top** for running processes. Mastering these commands means you can diagnose issues independently instead of escalating every problem to senior devs.

sections.title: Complete Debugging Workflow for a Failing Container
Key Points
content: **docker logs**: First step in debugging — shows stdout/stderr including stack traces, startup messages, and runtime errors
**docker exec -it**: Opens interactive shell inside running container — use /bin/bash or /bin/sh depending on base image
**docker inspect**: Returns JSON with full container config — network settings, environment variables, mounts, and resource limits
**docker stats**: Shows real-time CPU, memory, and network I/O for each container — useful for diagnosing performance issues
**docker top**: Displays running processes inside the container — helps verify that your Java process is actually running
**Environment checking**: Inside container, run env to see all environment variables — often Spring Boot issues are caused by missing vars
**Container restart debugging**: If a container keeps restarting, docker logs shows output from all restart attempts, revealing recurring errors

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When debugging a Docker container, I follow a three-step process. First, I use docker logs to see what the application is outputting. That's where I'll find stack traces, connection errors, or startup failures. I usually add --tail 100 to avoid overwhelming output, or -f to follow logs in real time while I reproduce the issue. Second, if logs don't tell the whole story, I use docker exec -it to open a shell inside the running container. The command looks like docker exec -it order-api /bin/bash. Once inside, I can check things like environment variables with env, verify files exist with ls, or see if the Java process is actually running with ps aux. This is really useful when the app starts but behaves strangely — maybe a config file is missing or permissions are wrong. Third, I use docker inspect to see the full container configuration as JSON. That's helpful for network debugging because it shows IP addresses, port mappings, and environment variables all in one place. One thing that's helped me is docker stats, which shows real-time CPU and memory usage. If a container is using a hundred percent CPU or running out of memory, that's a clear signal. Docker top is similar — it lists the processes running inside the container, so I can verify that my Java application actually started. A common mistake I see is trying to docker exec into a container that's already crashed. That won't work because exec needs a running container. In that case, docker logs is your only option to see what happened before it died.

groups.text: First stop for any broken container. Shows everything Spring Boot printed to stdout including startup errors and stack traces. Add -f to follow live.

beats.text: docker stats shows live CPU and memory usage for all running containers. If your Spring Boot app is eating memory, docker stats reveals it before you even connect a profiler.
